item.title: U.S. Sanctions Dismantle the Iranian Regime’s Revenue Streams
item.dc:creator: Thomas "Tommy" Pigott, SpokesmanOffice of the Spokesperson
item.description:
Thomas "Tommy" Pigott, SpokesmanOffice of the Spokesperson

U.S. Sanctions Dismantle the Iranian Regime’s Revenue Streams

Press Statement

September 4, 2026

The United States remains committed to cutting off the Iranian regime’s access to the international financial system and the resources it uses to destabilize the region and threaten U.S. interests and partners. Today’s U.S. Department of the Treasury sanctions on Türkiye-based Golden Global Bank mark the latest step in Operation Economic Outcast, a whole-of-government effort to sever the networks that allow the regime to launder funds, evade sanctions, and finance its terrorist proxies across the Middle East.

This action sends a clear message to financial institutions worldwide: facilitating Iran’s illicit financial activity carries serious consequences. This demonstrates the Trump Administration’s commitment to eliminating resources the regime uses to threaten regional stability, support terrorism, and advance its military capabilities.

The United States will continue to use every diplomatic and economic tool at its disposal to isolate the Iranian regime until it abandons its support for terrorism and its destabilizing activities in the region. We urge the international community to join this effort and ensure no institution serves as a financial lifeline for a regime that threatens peace and security.

Today’s action is being taken pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 13902, which targets the financial sector of Iran’s economy and advances Operation Economic Outcast—a campaign to completely isolate the regime from the financial lifelines that sustain its malign behavior. Please see the Department of the Treasury’s Press Release.

item.title: Secretary Rubio’s Travel to Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru
item.dc:creator: Thomas "Tommy" Pigott, SpokesmanOffice of the Spokesperson
item.description:
Thomas "Tommy" Pigott, SpokesmanOffice of the Spokesperson

Secretary Rubio’s Travel to Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru

Press Statement

September 4, 2026

Secretary of State Marco Rubio will travel to Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru from September 8-10 to strengthen key U.S. partnerships in our region. During the trip, he will meet with the new De La Espriella government in Colombia, President Noboa in Ecuador, and the new Fujimori government in Peru to discuss U.S. support for Colombia’s earthquake response; enhanced cooperation in the shared fight against narcoterrorism, which threatens our hemisphere; and the benefits of deeper commercial relationships between our countries.

Throughout the trip, the Secretary will reaffirm the Trump Administration’s commitment to a secure, prosperous, and democratic Western Hemisphere.

item.title: Quad Sherpas’ Meeting in New Delhi
item.dc:creator: Office of the Spokesperson
item.description:
Office of the Spokesperson

Quad Sherpas’ Meeting in New Delhi

Media Note

September 3, 2026

India’s Foreign Secretary Shri Vikram Misri hosted a Quad Sherpas’ Meeting in New Delhi on September 3, 2026. The meeting was attended by Ms. Elly Lawson, Deputy Secretary, Strategic Planning & Coordination Group, Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, Australia; Mr. Hiroyuki Namazu, Senior Deputy Minister for Foreign Affairs, Japan; and Mr. Sergio Gor, Special Envoy to South and Central Asia and Ambassador of USA to India.

The Quad Sherpas’ Meeting follows the Quad Foreign Ministers’ Meeting held in New Delhi on May 26, 2026 and was convened to take forward its outcomes and to prepare for the next Quad Foreign Ministers’ Meeting.

The Sherpas reviewed progress across ongoing Quad initiatives and discussed ways to further strengthen practical cooperation, with a shared commitment to advancing a free and open Indo-Pacific.

Discussions covered key areas of Quad cooperation, including maritime and transnational security; economic prosperity and security; critical and emerging technologies; and humanitarian assistance and emergency response. The Sherpas also exchanged views on developments in the Indo-Pacific and the broader regional and global context.

The Quad Sherpas reaffirmed the importance of focusing on concrete, action-oriented initiatives. They looked forward to continued consultations in the lead-up to the next Quad Foreign Ministers’ Meeting.

item.title: Further Sanctions on Cuba’s Elites, Financial Channels, and Resource Exploitation Apparatus
item.dc:creator: Marco Rubio, Secretary of State
item.description:
Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

Further Sanctions on Cuba’s Elites, Financial Channels, and Resource Exploitation Apparatus

Press Statement

September 3, 2026

The Communist Cuban regime continues to pose a deep, multifaceted threat to U.S. national security and our hemisphere’s stability. While the Cuban people suffer, the Castro family and their cronies in Cuba’s repressive Ministry of the Interior (MININT) continue to perpetuate their total control of the island’s economy, hoarding resources for the benefit of a small group of regime elites. Today, pursuant to President Trump’s Executive Order (E.O.) 14404, “Imposing Sanctions on Those Responsible for Repression in Cuba and for Threats to United States National Security and Foreign Policy,” I am designating five entities and one individual whose activities prop up the regime’s financial services, metals and mining, and energy sectors, and are part of networks that advance the regime’s threats to U.S. national security.

Among those designated today are a grandson of Raúl Castro, Fidel Ernesto Castro Calis, Banco Exterior de Cuba, and four entities exploiting Cuba’s natural resources or energy reserves for the benefit of the regime.

These designations reflect President Trump’s unwavering vision for a free Cuba — one where the regime’s illicit financial networks, repressive apparatuses, and entrenched Castro-era power structures are dismantled, and where the Cuban people, not their oppressors, inherit the nation’s future.

The Department’s actions are being taken pursuant to E.O. 14404, which authorizes sweeping sanctions on Cuba, including against persons who support the Cuban regime’s security apparatus and those responsible for repression in Cuba and other threats to U.S. national security.  These actions also further both E.O. 14380, “Addressing Threats to the United States by the Government of Cuba” and National Security Presidential Memorandum 5, which directs the Executive Branch to improve human rights, encourage the rule of law, foster free markets and free enterprise, and promote democracy in Cuba.  For more information on today’s action, see the Department of State’s Fact Sheet.

item.title: Secretary of State Marco Rubio at the Trump Administration’s Foundry School Launch
item.dc:creator: Marco Rubio, Secretary of State
item.description:
Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

Washington, D.C.

Donald J. Trump Institute of Peace

Secretary of State Marco Rubio at the Trump Administration’s Foundry School Launch

Remarks

September 3, 2026

UNDER SECRETARY HELBERG: Every so often, history hands a nation a choice: to drift, or to build. And every so often, it hands that nation a leader who inspires people to reject the drifters and build with boldness and confidence in the future.

One of our guests this morning is the son of Cuban exiles, a man whose family fled a regime that confiscated everything, and who grew up understanding in his bones that freedom and prosperity are not inherited – they’re defended, and they’re built. That heritage made him clear-eyed, and it gave him something rare in Washington: the memory of what it costs when a country loses its future.

For decades in the United States Senate, he warned us. He warned us that we traded our industrial base for the illusion of cheap abundance. He warned us that supply chains had become weapons pointed at us. And this year in Munich, in a speech that will be studied for a generation, he said what no Secretary of State had dared to say – that deindustrialization was a choice, and that reindustrialization must now be ours. He called on the free world not merely to defend Western civilization but to build a new Western century.

Under President Trump’s leadership, he has turned that vision into policy, restoring American economic strength as the foundation of economic power, and reminding the world that the arsenal of democracy was never a metaphor – it was a factory floor. He’s a statesman, a patriot, and the driving force behind the most consequential renewal of American economic statecraft since the Second World War.

Ladies and gentlemen, please join me in welcoming the 72nd Secretary of State of the United States, Secretary Marco Rubio. (Applause.)

SECRETARY RUBIO: Thank you. Thank you, all of you, first of all, for being here today. Thank you – Jacob Helberg’s doing a phenomenal job. Everybody at our department is doing a great job, and I’m very proud of the work the State Department is putting in into these and other initiatives.

One of the things we really wanted to do in our time here, and one of the reasons behind many of the reforms we undertook, is to allow us to have a State Department that could move at the speed of relevance, which is something we used to say all the time. Now it’s become almost a cliche, but it really is important – because world affairs are moving so quickly, economic developments are moving so quickly, and so much of that is internationalized, and it involves what we do around the world as well.

And so, I’m very proud of everybody at the Department of State and all the work that they’re doing to be a part of this initiative, along with our partners in the other agencies, because this truly is an interagency challenge that we’re facing.

What is the challenge that we’re here to talk about today? Let me put it to you this way: I think we made a terrible mistake in this country – not – many years ago, under people that were in charge at the time, especially at the end of the Cold War. And that was the idea that the ability to make things no longer mattered. And no matter – it didn’t matter any longer where things were made. They were to be made in the most efficient place at the lowest possible cost. That meant more profits for the company, lower costs for the consumers, and that was the way the world would work. There was this fantasy, really, that the whole world would become a free enterprise, democracies, and that everyone would look us.

That ran into reality – the reality that that is not how human events have ever worked, that the nation-state still does matter, nationalism is still real, national borders still matter, and that countries are going to always act in their best interest. But the result of it is that it deindustrialized America. We lost our ability and our capacity to make things, and not just big things – not just the kinds of big machinery and things that we normally identify with industry – but even some of the most basic components that are necessary, that underpin economic life, especially in the 21st century.

And we woke up to the reality just a few years ago that we are suddenly, as a nation, dangerously dependent – dangerously dependent – on other nations for all sorts of things that we need, not simply for our economic vibrancy but, in many cases, for our national security and our very survival as a prosperous nation-state. And so now we are involved in this endeavor across the board to try to reverse those mistakes. And it will be the work of multiple administrations, but it starts here and it starts now with this one that is receiving attention at its highest level.

One way is just the basic ingredients that go into all this, and it’s why you’ve seen such a focus on access to not just critical minerals as raw material but also to the ability to process them. But the other is – has to be the ability to actually make things once again. And we have to understand that re-industrialization, that 21st century industrial activity is going to look different than it did in the 20th century. It’s going to involve far more skills. It’s going to involve – not just are our workers going to have to be better educated in what they’re doing, but in many cases, given the evolution and the rapidly changing dynamics of the modern world, they may have to be retrained multiple times in their career.

One of the crown jewels that have powered American innovation and, ultimately, powered American economic influence and power around the world has been our system of higher education. It has produced extraordinary research; it has produced extraordinary breakthroughs. I think the sad part about it is the number of things we have innovated or created, but then they’re made somewhere else. And so, I think in the 21st century, this partnership with higher education is important, and it’s important for two reasons.

First of all, why build it when – why build a new wheel when we already have a wheel? We just need to repurpose that wheel to become the place where 21st century American workers go to become empowered with the skills they need to succeed. But I also think it’s important for higher education, and we’ve got some great partners here today that are already part of this initiative, and, of course, we want this partnership to grow to include other schools as well.

But I think it’s also important for higher education because, increasingly, young Americans are asking: Is the college degree worth it? Is the college route worth it? Because we have to borrow money or we have to spend money or we have to do all these sorts of things and, in the end, I get a degree, and all that degree does is either a) qualify me to get another degree or b) it may not even really lead to a job necessarily that’s different from the one I could have gotten otherwise.

And I think this speaks to that, because it also – in addition to being good for our country – is an opportunity to say to students: If you come here and you go to school and you follow this curriculum, you will leave here not just with a paper credential but with the skills that make you immediately employable in a high-paying job, in a good-paying job with long-term stability. And so this partnership is critical because what I hope it means, what I hope it symbolizes – and not just symbolizes but what I hope it is evidence of – is how government partnering with non-government entities like our higher education system and the private sector, the combination of those three pillars – the private sector that needs the workers and knows what they need from the workers; the higher education system that can equip young Americans with the skills they need to fill those jobs; and government that ensures not just that it’s acting as a convening body, but ensures that our national policies reflect these priorities. These three pillars working together drive us towards this outcome that we want, and it’s very important.

So, I think today is a great way to kick this off. We have great partners on board already. We hope to attract more. I want to thank all of you for being a part of it. And I – the last thing I want to say about this is that we understand that for this to work, this is not a two-year project. This is not a two-and-a-half-year project. This is a project that will involve sustainment for the long term. Multiple American administrations are going to have to make this a priority, which is why it’s so important that you see evidence that, at the highest levels of our government, now and for the future, you have that commitment.

And it’s why it’s exciting for us to have the Vice President here today to speak about it, because I think the evidence is not just the importance this administration gives it, but our acknowledgement that this is an issue that’s going to require long-term and sustained attention. This has to be an endeavor that goes on beyond the next two years. It has to go on for a generation. And I think having the Vice President here today with us is evidence of that commitment.

And so now I want to introduce and welcome to the stage here at the Institute of Peace, a beautiful building that the State Department’s using a lot – and we thank you all for coming – the Vice President of the United States of America, JD Vance. (Applause.)

Office of the Spokesperson

Further Sanctions on Cuba’s Elites, Financial Channels, and Resource Exploitation Apparatus

Fact Sheet

September 3, 2026

Today, the Department of State is designating five entities and one individual to further the Trump Administration’s comprehensive push to end the Cuban regime’s malign activities, both in Cuba and across our hemisphere. This action includes imposing sanctions on an additional member of the Castro family and further restricts the regime’s ability to fund and resource its repression.

All Department of State targets sanctioned today have been designated pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 14404, which authorizes sanctions on foreign persons determined to meet specified criteria related to repression in Cuba and other threats to U.S. national security and foreign policy.

Continued Designations of the Castro Regime

FIDEL ERNESTO CASTRO CALIS (CASTRO CALIS), grandson of Raul Modesto Castro Ruz, is being designated pursuant to Sec. 2(a)(i)(I) of E.O. 14404 for being an adult family member of ALEJANDRO CASTRO ESPIN (CASTRO ESPIN), a person designated pursuant to this order. CASTRO ESPIN, who is CASTRO CALIS’s father, was designated alongside CASTRO CALIS’s brother, RAUL ALEJANDRO CASTRO CALIS, pursuant to E.O. 14404 on June 4, 2026.

Further Restricting the Regime’s Ability to Exploit the International Financial System

BANCO EXTERIOR DE CUBA, a Cuban state-owned bank that specializes in corporate banking, foreign-trade finance, and international transactions, is being designated pursuant to Sec. 2(a)(i)(A) of E.O. 14404 for operating in or having operated in the financial services sector of the Cuban economy.

Cuban Entities Exploiting the Metals and Mining Sector

The following entities associated with the exploitation of Cuba’s metals and mining sector for the regime’s benefit are being designated pursuant to Sec. 2(a)(i)(A) of E.O. 14404 for operating in or having operated in the metals and mining sector of the Cuban economy:

  • EMPRESA DE SERVICIOS COMANDANTE RENE RAMOS LATOUR (NICAROTEC), which is a Cuban state-owned industrial and technical services enterprise which provides geological and mining support for the Cuban nickel sector.

item.title: Trump Administration Launches Foundry School to Build the Workforce Behind America’s Manufacturing Comeback
item.dc:creator: Office of the Spokesperson
item.description:
Office of the Spokesperson

Trump Administration Launches Foundry School to Build the Workforce Behind America’s Manufacturing Comeback

Fact Sheet

September 3, 2026

Vice President J.D. Vance and Secretary Marco Rubio announced today the launch of Foundry School, a training program for entrepreneurs, engineers, technicians, and industrial leaders to rebuild American manufacturing.  Under Secretary for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg hosted the event at the Donald J. Trump Institute of Peace, joined by presidents and senior leaders from the eight universities working to deliver the Foundry School curriculum and chief executives and company presidents from manufacturing and technology companies.

Putting American Workers First

President Trump’s reindustrialization agenda has already brought trillions of dollars in industrial investment to American soil.  Foundry School will focus on turning that investment into jobs.  American manufacturers will need an estimated 3.8 million skilled workers by 2033 in semiconductors, defense, energy, and beyond.  The State Department, working with Congress, plans to support the participation of Pax Silica economies in Foundry School and is working with Stanford University to develop the curriculum for U.S. and foreign participants.  Foundry School will collaborate with Pax Silica economies to create opportunities for America and partners in industries critical to our nation’s economic security. 

A Historic Workforce Development Program

Foundry School is anchored in a first-of-its-kind advanced manufacturing curriculum developed by Stanford University that also features keystone lectures provided by seven universities with which Stanford University has collaborated:  Arizona State University, Georgia Institute of Technology, The Ohio State University, The Pennsylvania State University, the University of Kansas, Vanderbilt University, and Washington University in St. Louis.  Across these eight campuses, the program will run 17 sessions, each taught by founders and CEOs from advanced manufacturing enterprises.  These industry leaders will be drawn from the United States and Pax Silica participants, including the Republic of Korea, Japan, Taiwan, and India, covering everything it takes to build and run a world-class manufacturing enterprise.  

Cutting Edge Curriculum

Foundry School is intended to close gaps in design and manufacturing capacity.  The curriculum will unfold in two phases.  Seven regional sessions, beginning in September 2026 and hosted by Arizona State University, Georgia Institute of Technology, The Ohio State University, The Pennsylvania State University, the University of Kansas, Vanderbilt University, and Washington University in St. Louis, will cover the fundamentals of modern factory design, materials and supply chains, assembly-line engineering, plant economics, regulation and permitting, and workforce development at scale.  A ten-session core program hosted by Stanford University, beginning in January 2027, will build on that foundation with advanced manufacturing capabilities, including precision tooling, industrial automation, quality systems, new product introduction, digital manufacturing, capital equipment, energy, global site selection, and defense production, concluding with a capstone session on lessons from failed manufacturing ventures.  Together, the 17 sessions form a one-of-a-kind curriculum.

A Flagship Initiative of Pax Silica

Foundry School is a flagship initiative of Pax Silica, the Trump Administration’s economic security partnership connecting governments, industry, and universities to strengthen the critical supply chains and industrial capabilities that underpin the AI economy.  Foundry School connects students and workers directly with the companies building and operating advanced manufacturing facilities.

For media inquiries, please submit a request.  For further information for universities and companies, contact FoundrySchool@state.gov.

item.title: San Marino National Day
item.dc:creator: Marco Rubio, Secretary of State
item.description:
Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

San Marino National Day

Press Statement

September 3, 2026

On behalf of the United States of America, I extend warm congratulations to the people of San Marino as you mark your National Day, commemorating the Feast of Saint Marinus and the founding of the world’s oldest republic.

San Marino’s remarkable endurance, even as the map of Europe was redrawn time and again, speaks to its deep-rooted commitment to liberty, independence, and perseverance.

The friendship between the United States and San Marino remains strong, grounded in a mutual respect for sovereignty and the right of nations to determine their own path. We look forward to deepening this partnership in the years to come.

On this occasion, the United States stands with you in celebration, extending best wishes for a joyful Feast of Saint Marinus and lasting prosperity in the years ahead.

item.title: Secretary of State Marco Rubio with Sergio Novelli on Al Día Con Sergio Novelli
item.dc:creator: Marco Rubio, Secretary of State
item.description:
Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

Via Teleconference

Secretary of State Marco Rubio with Sergio Novelli on Al Día Con Sergio Novelli

Interview

September 1, 2026

(Via translation.)

QUESTION:  We have with us the Secretary of State Marco Rubio who we’re going to talk about current events.  One of the biggest stories making headlines right now is the oil agreement announced by the President of the United States, Donald Trump.  Secretary, I wanted to ask you, did you participate directly in that negotiation, that agreement between the United States and Venezuela?  In other words, has the agreement already been signed?  Is it legally binding?  When will we be able to see the details of this document?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Of course.  But, well, first, obviously I participated.  And it is an important part of Venezuela’s transition and the country’s recovery.  There is still much more to be done.  The issues of democracy and elections are important.  All of that works together.  In terms of the figures, well, yesterday, we, a document was issued with many details about exactly what – this really is not an agreement with the interim government. It is an agreement with a private company with which the United States is participating together, obviously through the system that exists at this time.  And our hope is that this creates a model for other investments that, at the end of the day, begin to normalize the way the Venezuelan economy operates.  The Venezuelan economy during the years of Chavismo had really become something controlled by a network of corruption of people who were stealing, including people and countries that were stealing Venezuela’s wealth. 

For example, Cuba was being given billions of dollars in value of barrels of oil.  China was paying very little for the oil; they were receiving it at a discount.  In the case of Russia, they were simply taking the oil as payment on debt.  And many friends of Maduro and others had also benefited.  And what Venezuela needs in the long term is not simply a republic, a democratically elected republic, but also a government and an economic system that function normally and in a way that benefits the people.  The resources, for example, the investments and the taxes paid on those investments, should go directly to helping the people and the legitimate government of a country, not to individuals connected to those in power.  So, all of that is important as part of this process.

QUESTION:  I’d like to clarify some points related to this agreement with this company, North American Blue Energy Partners, which we understand is controlled by controversial businessman Alejandro Betancourt and would play an important role in these seventeen oil fields.  My question is, who selected this company, and what due diligence process did the U.S. government conduct?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Of course.  Well, first, this company is the largest private company that Venezuela had in terms of production and it also has a track record of being able to produce oil.  And simply what this is now is an agreement with the U.S. government through the Department of War.  Because they – we have a special account that can take possession of certain percentages of these types of things, to normalize that system, so that then it can create this opportunity to expand the country’s production capacity.  Remember that, of these 17 fields, the vast majority were controlled by Chinese or Russian interests.  Most of these fields were in the hands of the Chinese and the Russians, and many of them were not even being used. 

Now what we have is a system in which this company is going to produce more, with the support of the United States, and will be able to attract the private investment necessary to invest in the production capacity of these fields.  That is going to produce, as they say in English, royalties, but payments to the government.  Which eventually will be a democratically elected government in a republic.  And that, in turn, will be able to be used to expand the government’s capacity, as it should be in a normal country.  In the past, unfortunately, the vast majority of the country’s wealth was stolen or given away to geopolitical interests that are contrary to the interests not only of the Venezuelan people, but specifically in my case, in the job that I have, the interests of this country, of the United States, and of our national security.

QUESTION:  Excuse me for insisting, but why this particular company?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  It is the second – it is the largest private company that exists, after Chevron.  But it is the largest that exists in terms of not only the number of fields they have, but also their production capacity.  On top of that, the vast majority of the other fields were not operating.  Many of these fields had been given away, for example, to individuals connected to the-to the regime, but they were not producing or were producing very little.  This is a company that has a track record of production, that has knowledge of the system, and now we have in place a whole series of laws and regulations that will regulate the way in which it is going to be professionalized.  This is going to become a professionalized operation with, with jurisdiction and laws that will apply to it so that the money is never used improperly or in a way – that is not adequate or appropriate.

QUESTION:  Now, but this company is linked to Alejandro Betancourt.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Correct.

QUESTION:  A person who has, let’s say, an extensive history, including investigations related to corruption in Venezuela and other countries.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, two things. First, we thoroughly investigate what we know within our system.  Obviously, if these individuals were under investigation in the United States, and we have checked that with all the authorities, there was no investigation within our system against him.  Second, unfortunately, when you look at these issues, it is complicated, right?  Because, on the other hand, he is also an individual who is already known, who provided a great deal of support, for example, during the time of Juan Guaidó. 

Before I entered this position, during President Trump’s first term in 2019, this was an individual who ended up in a very, very bad place with Maduro.  Because it became known that he was supporting elements of the opposition back in 2019, which even created problems for him with Maduro.  But now we have an opportunity to do something that I believe is going to benefit everyone.  But specifically, in the long term, benefit the Venezuelan people. 

And no – this is only one part of that.  Obviously, there are still – Venezuela’s oil reserves are enormous, and there are many private companies outside of this that also want to invest in the country and turn it into a professional system, a system that works the way it is supposed to work.  That is, they pay the government the royalties, as they say in English, and that money goes toward the capacity to build schools, roads, respond to earthquakes.  We saw at this time that the government, after – through years of stealing the money, did not even have the capacity to respond to a, a situation like the earthquake.  All of that has to happen as part of a recovery so that the country can begin to recover from 25 years of mismanagement and corruption.

QUESTION:  Yes. Now, how could we, or how could one, in any case, ensure that this money actually reaches the Venezuelan people, meets the needs of the Venezuelan people, and does not end up in corruption?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well.

QUESTION:  As in the last twenty-seven years.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Correct.  Two things.  In the short term, because this is part of a process.  This is not something that happens from one day to the next, but it is part of a process.  In the short term, as we well know, the United States has positioned itself in such a way that it can conduct, through KPMG, audits of all the money that is being generated at this time.  In the long term, the future of Venezuela is to have a democratically elected- elected government, in a republic where the country’s leaders are directly accountable to the laws of the country and to the voters of that country.  That is where we have to end up with this project.  At the end of the day, it is to have – what we have right now is an interim government that is functioning in that capacity because we do not want destabilization, we do not want violence, we do not want mass migration, we do not want any type of situation that could destabilize the country. 

And there is precedent for this in other countries that have gone through transitions.  You have to work with the authorities that exist at that time.  But our desire and our goal here is not to create a permanent system, for the current system to become the permanent system.  What we all want on our part, and we have insisted on this and have been very clear about it, is that at the end of the day, the time will come when Venezuela has to be governed by a democratically elected government.  But remember that democracy and a republic are not just about an election.  The election is obviously key, but that election has to be a valid election.  And the government that takes office, we do not want them to inherit an economic disaster, a country in disaster.  We want them to inherit a country that is stabilized and that has the – obviously, it is going to continue to have problems, but that it doesn’t have a crisis situation.

QUESTION:  Exactly.  Because that would be, in any case, the possibility of holding free elections in Venezuela very soon.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  No, but that has to happen.  Everyone here understands that it has to happen.  Because at the end of the day, Venezuela cannot get to where it needs to be without having a legitimate government, a government that complies with all international standards, that can receive the necessary recognition.  Even investors are going to want to see that, they are going to want to know that the system that exists is the same.  Look, for example, no country is perfect, but in this country everyone knows that in the United States there are a series of laws and courts and a judicial branch, legislative branch, an executive branch.  And even though the leaders change, at the end of the day, the law and the system remain the same.  That type of, that type of stability is necessary for a country to move forward. 

What happens is, as has happened in other cases, for example, you look at the case of Nicaragua, where they held elections almost immediately and they won.  The opposition won. But a few years later, Sandinismo returned and took control of the country and they lost their freedom. We do not want that here.  We want a permanent democracy and republic for the future of Venezuela.  But you have to understand, we are – Venezuela is still recovering from more than 20-some years of a system that has been corrupted and does not work.

QUESTION:  Is there a deadline for those elections?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, for me, it would be as soon as possible. Obviously, the conditions have to exist, and those conditions have to be created. For example, at this very moment, if there were elections in Venezuela tomorrow, we would be using the existing machinery.  That machinery is not going to give you a system – it is not going to give you a valid election.

QUESTION:  So it has to be cleaned up.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  But it is – well, for example, the opposition parties.  They need room, space, time, and resources to be able to organize themselves as a political movement. We are talking about movements that for the last several years have had to demonstrate in the streets as a protest movement. Now they have to become a political movement that can conduct a campaign.  We have to have a free, open press so that all the candidates can express themselves. We have to have a National Electoral Council that everyone accepts as a legitimate council.  We have to have voting machinery that everyone knows has not been tampered with.  We have to have international elements from abroad that oversee and give their approval, their seal of approval, to those elections.  All of that is necessary. 

We have to create the conditions for that, including security.  Nor can we have situations in which, look, an interesting case that is happening right now in the hemisphere, the case of Bolivia as well.  There were elections, the current president won, but he has now faced a whole series of very serious problems because the country is still recovering from years and years of mismanagement.

We do not want that for Venezuela.  We want that when there are elections in Venezuela, which God willing will be as soon as possible, those elections do not-not simply a democratically elected government, but a government that is not inheriting a total and complete disaster.  Because then it is going to make the task of creating that lasting republic even more difficult.  And finally, I will tell you that efforts are already underway to make that happen.  For example, next month, members of the leadership of the 2015 National Assembly, which we have recognized in the past as the legitimate government of the country, will meet again. And those negotiations, we – it is up to the Venezuelans, but we are going to do everything possible to continue facilitating those negotiations.

QUESTION:  Yes, of course.  That is exactly what leads me to ask you, Secretary, about María Corina Machado, who has emerged as a leader par excellence at this time in Venezuela, and she has reiterated that she wants to return to the country.  In fact, she said, yesterday she said that she has a clear, clear plan to return.  My question is, would she have to receive the approval of the United States in order to return to Venezuela?  Or can she do so?  Why?  Because —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  No. María Corina Machado, a Venezuelan citizen, has every right to enter her country whenever she wants to return.  We have given her advice.  For example, during the earthquake, we had many concerns and will continue to have concerns in the future, but we want her safety to be guaranteed.  But, in any event, she has every right to return.  She is a Venezuelan citizen.  She is Venezuelan. She is not Panamanian, she is not American, she is Venezuelan and she can – but it is not only María Corina, whom I greatly admire.

There are also other important political figures from the past who have had to go into exile.  We understand that at this time many of the leaders, for example, who I (in the years 2014, 2015, 2016, 2017), when I was the only one here talking about Venezuela in Washington, many of the figures we dealt with back then are outside the country.  They still have not returned to the country.  It is important that all of those individuals, if they want to, be able to return and participate in Venezuela’s political life in a way that does not put them in danger and that they are given the necessary space to participate.  As they have the right, as Venezuelan citizens, to participate in the future of Venezuela.  If they wish to do so.

QUESTION:  Could she return as soon as tomorrow?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  That is up to her.  We cannot prevent her from traveling anywhere.

QUESTION:  No, of course.  But would the government provide her with security, provide security for her?

Secretary of State Marco Rubio with Sergio Novelli on Al Día Con Sergio Novelli

Interview

September 1, 2026

(Via translation.)

QUESTION:  We have with us the Secretary of State Marco Rubio who we’re going to talk about current events.  One of the biggest stories making headlines right now is the oil agreement announced by the President of the United States, Donald Trump.  Secretary, I wanted to ask you, did you participate directly in that negotiation, that agreement between the United States and Venezuela?  In other words, has the agreement already been signed?  Is it legally binding?  When will we be able to see the details of this document?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Of course.  But, well, first, obviously I participated.  And it is an important part of Venezuela’s transition and the country’s recovery.  There is still much more to be done.  The issues of democracy and elections are important.  All of that works together.  In terms of the figures, well, yesterday, we, a document was issued with many details about exactly what – this really is not an agreement with the interim government. It is an agreement with a private company with which the United States is participating together, obviously through the system that exists at this time.  And our hope is that this creates a model for other investments that, at the end of the day, begin to normalize the way the Venezuelan economy operates.  The Venezuelan economy during the years of Chavismo had really become something controlled by a network of corruption of people who were stealing, including people and countries that were stealing Venezuela’s wealth. 

For example, Cuba was being given billions of dollars in value of barrels of oil.  China was paying very little for the oil; they were receiving it at a discount.  In the case of Russia, they were simply taking the oil as payment on debt.  And many friends of Maduro and others had also benefited.  And what Venezuela needs in the long term is not simply a republic, a democratically elected republic, but also a government and an economic system that function normally and in a way that benefits the people.  The resources, for example, the investments and the taxes paid on those investments, should go directly to helping the people and the legitimate government of a country, not to individuals connected to those in power.  So, all of that is important as part of this process.

QUESTION:  I’d like to clarify some points related to this agreement with this company, North American Blue Energy Partners, which we understand is controlled by controversial businessman Alejandro Betancourt and would play an important role in these seventeen oil fields.  My question is, who selected this company, and what due diligence process did the U.S. government conduct?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Of course.  Well, first, this company is the largest private company that Venezuela had in terms of production and it also has a track record of being able to produce oil.  And simply what this is now is an agreement with the U.S. government through the Department of War.  Because they – we have a special account that can take possession of certain percentages of these types of things, to normalize that system, so that then it can create this opportunity to expand the country’s production capacity.  Remember that, of these 17 fields, the vast majority were controlled by Chinese or Russian interests.  Most of these fields were in the hands of the Chinese and the Russians, and many of them were not even being used. 

Now what we have is a system in which this company is going to produce more, with the support of the United States, and will be able to attract the private investment necessary to invest in the production capacity of these fields.  That is going to produce, as they say in English, royalties, but payments to the government.  Which eventually will be a democratically elected government in a republic.  And that, in turn, will be able to be used to expand the government’s capacity, as it should be in a normal country.  In the past, unfortunately, the vast majority of the country’s wealth was stolen or given away to geopolitical interests that are contrary to the interests not only of the Venezuelan people, but specifically in my case, in the job that I have, the interests of this country, of the United States, and of our national security.

QUESTION:  Excuse me for insisting, but why this particular company?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  It is the second – it is the largest private company that exists, after Chevron.  But it is the largest that exists in terms of not only the number of fields they have, but also their production capacity.  On top of that, the vast majority of the other fields were not operating.  Many of these fields had been given away, for example, to individuals connected to the-to the regime, but they were not producing or were producing very little.  This is a company that has a track record of production, that has knowledge of the system, and now we have in place a whole series of laws and regulations that will regulate the way in which it is going to be professionalized.  This is going to become a professionalized operation with, with jurisdiction and laws that will apply to it so that the money is never used improperly or in a way – that is not adequate or appropriate.

QUESTION:  Now, but this company is linked to Alejandro Betancourt.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Correct.

QUESTION:  A person who has, let’s say, an extensive history, including investigations related to corruption in Venezuela and other countries.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, two things. First, we thoroughly investigate what we know within our system.  Obviously, if these individuals were under investigation in the United States, and we have checked that with all the authorities, there was no investigation within our system against him.  Second, unfortunately, when you look at these issues, it is complicated, right?  Because, on the other hand, he is also an individual who is already known, who provided a great deal of support, for example, during the time of Juan Guaidó. 

Before I entered this position, during President Trump’s first term in 2019, this was an individual who ended up in a very, very bad place with Maduro.  Because it became known that he was supporting elements of the opposition back in 2019, which even created problems for him with Maduro.  But now we have an opportunity to do something that I believe is going to benefit everyone.  But specifically, in the long term, benefit the Venezuelan people. 

And no – this is only one part of that.  Obviously, there are still – Venezuela’s oil reserves are enormous, and there are many private companies outside of this that also want to invest in the country and turn it into a professional system, a system that works the way it is supposed to work.  That is, they pay the government the royalties, as they say in English, and that money goes toward the capacity to build schools, roads, respond to earthquakes.  We saw at this time that the government, after – through years of stealing the money, did not even have the capacity to respond to a, a situation like the earthquake.  All of that has to happen as part of a recovery so that the country can begin to recover from 25 years of mismanagement and corruption.

QUESTION:  Yes. Now, how could we, or how could one, in any case, ensure that this money actually reaches the Venezuelan people, meets the needs of the Venezuelan people, and does not end up in corruption?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well.

QUESTION:  As in the last twenty-seven years.

We have to create the conditions for that, including security.  Nor can we have situations in which, look, an interesting case that is happening right now in the hemisphere, the case of Bolivia as well.  There were elections, the current president won, but he has now faced a whole series of very serious problems because the country is still recovering from years and years of mismanagement.
